profiles.meeting_scenario: A university-affiliated innovation lab has been asked by a home-appliance manufacturer to design a one-day internal workshop on new kitchen food-waste solutions, and the lab is considering structuring the ideation around three expression modes: spoken-only, sketch-based, and object-based. In this brainstorming meeting, the two leads are generating candidate formats for a small pre-launch pilot that could later become both a sponsor-facing workshop method and a comparative internal study. The agenda is to sketch several workable session formats, decide how the three variants should differ, and identify what would make the pilot useful. The expected outcome is a short list of candidate workshop designs and a shared sense that they have aligned on what the pilot should accomplish.

members.name: Elena Rossi
members.expertise: Facilitation, industrial design methods, concept development workshops
members.background: Elena trained in industrial design and now runs co-creation sessions for corporate and public-sector clients, with a track record of turning rough workshop outputs into tangible concept directions.
members.private_state: She wants the pilot to impress the sponsor and yield at least a few concept directions that can be carried into a paid follow-on engagement, while still sounding rigorous enough for the research-minded team.
hidden_assumptions: A pilot workshop is only worth running if it produces at least some concepts that could plausibly move into downstream prototyping.
When people say an idea meets the requirements, they mainly mean it answers the design brief constraints such as footprint, user need, and installation limits.
An object-based session works best when participants can improvise with whatever physical materials feel suggestive in the moment rather than with tightly standardized kits.
A more resolved idea is one with enough form, mechanism, and use-context detail that a design team could sketch a next-step prototype from it.

members.name: Daniel Cho
members.expertise: Experimental design, protocol analysis, creativity studies, coding reliability
members.background: Daniel has a background in organizational psychology and HCI research, and he specializes in turning workshop activity into analyzable data through structured observation and transcript coding.
members.private_state: He wants a methodologically clean pilot that can calibrate timings, coding rules, and comparison logic without introducing uncontrolled variation that would make the results hard to defend internally or publish later.
hidden_assumptions: A pilot is primarily a shakedown run for instruments, timings, and coding procedures; concept quality is secondary at this stage.
Requirements include not only the product brief but also the experimental constraints needed for fair comparison across expression modes.
An object-based condition should use identical, pre-specified component kits so that differences come from expression mode rather than material variation.
A more resolved idea is one that can be segmented, labeled, and linked consistently by coders, even if it is not yet concrete enough for downstream prototyping.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to the upcoming session as a "pilot" and talk about making it useful before the full rollout.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks the pilot should function as a sponsor-visible dry run that generates a few promising concept directions and demonstrates the value of the workshop format.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks the pilot is mainly a calibration exercise for timings, coding rules, and condition comparability, even if the ideas themselves are not especially promising.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In normal workplace talk, "pilot" naturally covers both rehearsal and learning, so each hears the other's comments as compatible with their own version of usefulness.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as meeting the requirements
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say they want ideas that "meet the requirements" of the food-waste brief.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 includes the appliance sponsor's design-brief constraints, such as fitting under a standard sink cabinet, avoiding plumbing changes, and feeling realistic for renters.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 includes those design-brief constraints but also folds in study-design requirements such as comparable prompts, balanced time allocation, and outputs that can be coded across conditions.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Because the phrase "requirements" sounds fully shared and professional, neither person notices that one is talking about solution requirements while the other quietly includes protocol requirements in the same bundle.

misalignment_points.topic: How the object-based variant will work
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree that one condition should use "pieces" or "rudimentary objects" instead of just talking or sketching.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 imagines a table of mixed foam blocks, clips, tubing, cardboard rings, and kitchen odds and ends that participants can appropriate freely to think with and combine however they like.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 imagines identical trays containing the same numbered set of components for every team, so object manipulation remains standardized and comparable across sessions.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: They both endorse the same high-level method label, and the exact composition of the object materials feels like a minor setup detail rather than a strategic choice worth unpacking in a brainstorming meeting.

misalignment_points.topic: What a more resolved idea looks like
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say they hope the object-based variant will produce "more resolved" or "higher-resolution" ideas.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means concepts that specify enough physical form, user interaction, and mechanism that a designer could immediately turn them into a first prototype sketch or mock-up.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means ideas expressed clearly enough that coders can identify distinct idea units, trace links between them, and rate requirement fit without ambiguity.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds like shared praise for idea quality, and each interpretation is reasonable in a design-research setting, so the difference stays invisible during cooperative discussion.

turns.inner_thought: If we're going to call this a pilot, it needs to look and feel like a credible mini-version of the sponsor workshop, not just a lab exercise. I want enough energy in the room that we come away with at least a couple of concept directions we can point to later. And the three modes can't blur together; if object-based is in there, it should visibly shift the kind of thinking people do.
turns.utterance: Okay, so for today I'd love us to shape the pilot in a way that feels genuinely useful before we roll anything out more broadly. And I think the three expression modes need to feel meaningfully different—otherwise we'll learn very little from running spoken, sketch, and object-based versions side by side.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, exactly: useful means we can tell whether the structure holds up and whether the comparison logic is defensible. If the pilot exposes timing problems, unclear prompts, or messy outputs, that's a success even if the concepts are mediocre. I need enough control that when we scale, we're not dragging hidden variability with us.
turns.utterance: I agree. For me the pilot should give us a clean read on which format is easiest to compare before we scale it up. If we can use it to tighten the structure and see where the modes really diverge, that puts us in a much stronger position.

turns.inner_thought: Best to ground all three in the same sponsor brief: under-sink, renter-friendly, no major installation drama. Then we can actually see which mode helps people generate ideas that fit the real-world constraints the client cares about. If the outputs don't meet the requirements in that practical sense, the exercise won't impress anyone.
turns.utterance: I think we anchor all three on exactly the same food-waste challenge—something renter-friendly, under-sink, and easy to grasp—so we're not changing the brief itself. Then we can look at which kinds of ideas best meet the requirements without the challenge moving around underneath us.

turns.inner_thought: Same brief is necessary, but not sufficient. We also need the prompt wording, the time blocks, and the form of output aligned enough that 'meeting the requirements' means something comparable across conditions. Otherwise any difference could come from procedure instead of mode.
turns.utterance: Yes, and if we do that, I'd also want the prompts, timing, and outputs aligned enough that we're seeing the requirements being met in a comparable way across the three conditions. That way any differences are easier to interpret.

turns.inner_thought: For the object round, I want a generous spread of materials people can grab intuitively—tubing, collars, clips, foam chunks, maybe a few odd kitchen-like forms. The point is to let them improvise and discover mechanisms through handling, not force them through a constrained assembly task.
turns.utterance: For the object-based round, I can imagine teams working with pieces on the table—things like tubing, cardboard collars, clips, foam forms, that kind of rudimentary object language—to think through mechanisms quickly rather than only describing them.

turns.inner_thought: Good, object manipulation could produce clearer externalization. But to keep the condition analyzable, every team should get the same numbered set of pieces in the same arrangement. That way the object-based variant stays standardized and any differences are attributable to mode, not material availability.
turns.utterance: I like the pieces idea a lot. If each team is working from the same kit, the object condition should stay much easier to compare, and we still get the benefit of people thinking with their hands instead of just talking.

turns.inner_thought: Exactly—spoken brainstorming usually generates lots of loose fragments, while working with objects tends to slow people down and force commitment. That's useful because the sponsor will care more about a handful of stronger concept directions they can picture taking forward than a wall full of half-formed ideas. If the pilot gives us that, it will earn its keep.
turns.utterance: My hunch is that, compared with spoken brainstorming, the object condition may give us fewer ideas but more resolved ones, which is often exactly what makes a pilot useful from the sponsor's perspective.

turns.inner_thought: More resolved would be great if it means the outputs are segmented clearly enough that coders can identify idea units and trace development without guessing. The object condition might naturally produce cleaner chains between fragments and elaborations, which would help reliability a lot.
turns.utterance: I can see that. More resolved concepts would help on my side too, especially if the outputs are distinct enough that coders can trace the links between ideas without having to do too much interpretation after the fact.

turns.inner_thought: The sketch mode can bridge the gap: broader than objects, but still concrete enough to test layouts, interactions, and rough physical logic. It's a good middle layer for checking whether concepts satisfy the brief constraints before they become too abstract or too locked-in.
turns.utterance: Then maybe the visual variant sits in the middle. Teams could sketch layouts and interactions, so it's not as open-ended as talk and not as tactile as objects, while still letting us see whether the concepts satisfy the brief's key constraints and become a bit more resolved.

turns.inner_thought: For the pilot, sample size can stay small as long as it's enough to test whether all three conditions can be administered consistently and scored using the same framework. I'm not chasing robust outcome claims yet; I need calibration and evidence that the protocol behaves.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. And for the pilot, I don't think we need a huge number of teams—just enough to see whether the three formats can be run consistently and whether the resulting material can be scored in the same way across conditions.

turns.inner_thought: I'll draft something that keeps the structure parallel enough for Daniel, but I need to preserve enough openness that participants can surprise us and land on concept directions with real potential. Especially in the object-based round, I don't want the setup to feel over-managed or it will flatten the ideas.
turns.utterance: Great. I'll draft a workshop flow that keeps the three modes parallel but still gives participants enough freedom to generate strong concepts. That should let the pilot do its job while preserving the character of each format.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect. I'll build an observation sheet and coding structure that captures requirement fit, idea links, and resolution level consistently across spoken, sketch, and object outputs. If we can get that framework stable in the pilot, the rest becomes much easier to defend later.
turns.utterance: And I'll put together the observation sheet and coding structure so we capture requirement fit and idea links across all three variants. If we do that well, the pilot should give us a solid base for the next round.
